title: The recited Qur'an on radio
hookLine: reciters like Abdul Basit reach millions by radio and records

lines: A RADIO ON A CAFÉ SHELF.
cards: A radio sits on a café shelf in a Cairo side street, turned low. A voice comes out of it, and the man wiping tables stops.
The voice climbs, holds one note for what feels like a full breath and then some, and comes down again on the last word of a verse. Somebody in the back murmurs Allah under their breath.
The same voice is coming out of a market stall in Karachi, a cassette player in a kitchen in Jakarta, a record player in Detroit. One man, reciting. Today: the recited Qur'an on radio.

teach.b: The Qur'an asks to be heard: "And when the Qur'an is recited, give ear to it and pay heed, that ye may obtain mercy." It also tells the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to "chant the Qur'an in measure."
For a long time, that meant one reciter and the people within earshot. A great voice could fill a mosque, but no further. Then came the radio and the record.
In Egypt, reciters were broadcast, and one of them, Sheikh Abdul Basit Abd us-Samad, became a voice that traveled far beyond Egypt.
Fans describe how long he could hold a breath, and his recitations travel still, on old records, cassettes and now phones. People hear two broad styles.

teach.h: ORNATE OR PLAIN, BOTH WITH TAJWID.
teach.b: One is slow and ornate, with long held notes, the kind that makes a whole room go quiet. The other is plainer and steadier, good for following along or learning by heart.
Both follow the careful rules of tajwid, which govern how each letter and pause is sounded.
A hadith in Abu Dawud tells believers to beautify the Qur'an with their voices. Radio didn't change the words.
It changed who could hear them: a farmer, a factory worker, a child in a city far from Cairo, all listening to the same voice at the same hour.

how: Muslims listen to recorded recitation at home, in cars and in shops, and Qur'an radio stations broadcast it through the day; listeners often fall quiet while it plays, following the verse that asks them to give ear.

games.why: Qur'an 7:204: "when the Qur'an is recited, give ear to it and pay heed, that ye may obtain mercy."

practice: If you can, play a short recording of Abdul Basit, perhaps al-Fatiha, the Qur'an's opening chapter, or simply remember any recitation you've heard.

Don't try to understand every word; listen the way the verse asks, give ear and pay heed, and notice where his voice rises, where it holds, where it lets go. Notice your own breath while he holds his.

wordCard.voice: Tajwid, the careful rules for sounding each letter and pause of the Qur'an, that reciters like Abdul Basit followed as radio carried their voices worldwide. Today's word.
